911.title: The Geonim
911.hook: heads of the Babylonian academies answer questions from Jews across the world
911.howItsDone: Jews today still turn to the Geonim's surviving letters and rulings as early witnesses to how the Talmud was read, and historians study the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon for its account of the Mishnah and Talmud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bavli, sealed with Rav Ashi and Ravina. Your line was the talmud sealed. Today, a new stretch of the story begins: Babylon, the Islamic world, and the first Ashkenazim.

A community in Kairouan, in North Africa, has a question it can't settle. Not about a holiday or a meal. A history question: how was the Mishnah written? And the Talmud, how did it come together? Who did what, and in what order? So Rabbi Jacob ben Nissim, a teacher there, writes a letter and sends it a very long way east, to the head of the academy at Pumbedita. And an answer comes back: long, careful, and so useful that people are still reading it.
screen: `A QUESTION IN KAIROUAN.` → `HOW WAS THE MISHNAH WRITTEN?` → `A LETTER EAST TO PUMBEDITA.`

segments.voice: After the Talmud was sealed, the academies of Sura and Pumbedita went on, and their heads came to carry a title: Gaon, in the plural Geonim. It's usually explained as short for the head of the academy that is the pride of Jacob, a phrase from a psalm, which in the 1917 Jewish translation reads "The pride of Jacob whom He loveth." In everyday Hebrew, gaon came to mean a genius. But here it's a job title, and the job was to teach, and to answer. Jewish communities were spread across a huge distance. The Talmud was their shared text, but it is long and hard, and real life keeps producing cases it never quite covered. So letters traveled to the Geonim, who read the question, studied it, and wrote back. The letter from Kairouan reached Rav Sherira Gaon, head of Pumbedita. His reply, known as the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, walks through how the Mishnah and the Talmud took shape, teacher by teacher. Here's the picture: letters across the world. A text sealed in one place, and a web of letters spreading it to many others; a question written in one city, an answer in another, and the conversation of the academies reaching people who had never seen them.
screen: `GAON: HEAD OF THE ACADEMY.` · `THE PRIDE OF JACOB.` · `THE LETTER OF RAV SHERIRA GAON.` · then, large: `LETTERS ACROSS THE WORLD.`

If you pray, you can bring that question to God as it is.

912.title: Questions and answers
912.hook: responsa, rulings sent by letter, a form of Jewish law that continues today
912.howItsDone: Jews with a question of Jewish law often ask a rabbi, and rabbis today still write formal teshuvot, citing the Talmud and earlier responsa, on new questions as they arise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Geonim, and a question from Kairouan answered by Rav Sherira Gaon. Your line was letters across the world. Today, the shape those letters took.

A prayer book that began as a reply. Tradition says a community in Spain wrote to Rav Amram, a Gaon of Sura, asking how the prayers of the year should be said. He wrote back with the order of the prayers, set out with their rules. That answer, known as the Order of Rav Amram, is remembered as one of the early written orders of Jewish prayer. Someone far away didn't know, so they asked. Someone else took the question seriously and answered in full. Today's word names that shape, and it already means something else in Hebrew.
screen: `A COMMUNITY IN SPAIN ASKS.` → `RAV AMRAM WRITES BACK.` → `A PRAYER BOOK BEGINS AS A REPLY.`

segments.voice: Teshuvot means answers; a single one is a teshuvah. The word is often heard as return, or repentance, the turning back to God of the High Holy Days. But the same Hebrew word also means a reply, a word that turns back to the one who asked. The Bible uses it that way. In the book of Job, Job tells his friends, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "as for your answers, there remaineth only faithlessness." The Hebrew word for answers there is the plural of teshuvah. In Jewish law, the full name of this form is she'elot u-teshuvot, questions and answers. In English it's called responsa. The shape is simple. At the top, the question: who is asking, what happened, what they need to know. Then the answer: the sources, the reasoning, and the ruling. It's written to a real person with a real problem, not to a textbook. That's what makes responsa precious to historians, too: tucked into the questions is ordinary life, a business deal gone wrong, a marriage, a quarrel between neighbors. And the form never stopped. Rabbis still write teshuvot about things no Gaon could have pictured, citing the Talmud, the Geonim, and everyone in between. Ask and answer.

913.title: Saadia Gaon
913.hook: a Gaon translates the Torah into Arabic and writes on faith and reason
913.howItsDone: Saadia's Arabic translation of the Torah is still read in some Yemenite Jewish communities alongside the Hebrew, and his Book of Beliefs and Opinions is studied in courses on Jewish thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teshuvot, the answers that crossed the world by letter. Your line was ask and answer. Today, a Gaon who took on questions about faith itself.

Believers whose belief is clouded. Doubters who are proud of doubting. And thoughtful people sinking, as he puts it, in a sea of confusion, with no one to pull them out. That's what one author sees when he looks around, and it worries him enough to write. Not a sermon: an argument, step by step, using reason, about what can be known and how. The author is Saadia, head of the academy at Sura. He's a Gaon, like the ones we met this week, but his questions aren't about one case of law. They're about whether faith and thinking can stand on the same ground.
screen: `A WORRIED AUTHOR.` → `PEOPLE SINKING IN CONFUSION.` → `SAADIA, GAON OF SURA.`

segments.voice: Saadia did two big things. First, he translated the Torah into Arabic, the everyday language of the Jews around him, and it has come down to us in Hebrew letters. It's often called his Tafsir, an Arabic word for explanation, because his translation explains as it goes. Second, he wrote the book from the hook, known in English as The Book of Beliefs and Opinions. In it he lays out how a person comes to know things: what the senses observe, what reason grasps, what you can necessarily infer, and reliable tradition, which for him includes the Torah. Here's his bold claim. Faith and reason don't compete. Rightly used, they lead to the same truth. Then he asks the obvious question back. If reason can reach it, why does anyone need revelation? His answer, in plain words: because thinking things through takes a long time, and some people never get there. Revelation gives the truth to everyone at once, the young and the busy included. Reason lets you understand it, test it, and defend it when someone challenges you. Not one instead of the other. His translation brought the Torah into the language of the street; his philosophy brought the street's hardest questions into the Torah.
screen: `THE TORAH IN ARABIC.` · `THE BOOK OF BELIEFS AND OPINIONS.` · then, large: `FAITH AND REASON, ONE TRUTH.` · `WHY REVELATION? IT REACHES EVERYONE.`

914.title: Jews in the Islamic world
914.hook: Baghdad, Cairo, Kairouan: long periods of flourishing, and times of hardship
914.howItsDone: Jewish communities with roots in North Africa, the Middle East and Yemen keep traditions, melodies and words from centuries of life in Arabic-speaking lands, and Judeo-Arabic texts are still studied.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saadia Gaon, who put the Torah into Arabic and argued that faith and reason lead to one truth. Your line was faith and reason. Today, the world he wrote from.

Kitab. It's the Arabic word for a book. Saadia's great work of philosophy has it in its Arabic title, and it shows up in a phrase the Qur'an uses for Jews and Christians: ahl al-kitab, the people of the book, or as one old translation puts it, the People of the Scripture. In the copies of Saadia's book that came down to us, kitab is spelled in Hebrew letters. Arabic words, Hebrew script: that way of writing is called Judeo-Arabic, a small window into a very big world. For centuries, from Baghdad to Cairo to Kairouan, Jewish life unfolded in lands ruled by Muslims, and in Arabic.
screen: `KITAB: A BOOK.` → `PEOPLE OF THE BOOK.` → `ARABIC WORDS, HEBREW LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The academies we've been following, Sura and Pumbedita, came to sit in a world governed by Muslim rulers, whose capital was Baghdad. Under Islamic law, Jews and Christians were usually treated as protected peoples, called dhimmi. They could keep their faith, their courts and their houses of worship. They also paid a special tax and lived under limits, and how those limits felt depended a great deal on who was in power. There were long stretches of flourishing. Jews worked as merchants, doctors, scholars and officials. They wrote poetry, philosophy and Bible commentary in Arabic, and their letters crossed seas because trade routes did. Jewish thinkers read Muslim philosophers and argued with them; ideas moved in both directions. That's the world Saadia wrote from. There were also hard times. In Cairo, for a time, a caliph ordered synagogues and churches torn down, before the policy was reversed. Some rulers enforced humiliating rules. Communities sometimes faced violence, and some had to flee. Both are true, and the honest history keeps both: neither perfect harmony nor constant persecution fits what the records show. Neighbors, business partners, rivals, sometimes victims, sometimes friends, living the long middle of history side by side, and writing it down in Arabic, in Hebrew letters.
screen: `PROTECTED, AND LIMITED.` · `LONG STRETCHES OF FLOURISHING.` · `AND TIMES OF HARDSHIP.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

915.title: The Cairo Geniza
915.hook: a storeroom where worn writings were kept, holding centuries of daily life
915.howItsDone: Synagogues and Jewish homes set aside worn prayer books, Bibles and other pages with God's name, and communities later bury them in a Jewish cemetery rather than throwing them away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dhimmi, and Jews among Muslims: flourishing and hardship, in Arabic in Hebrew letters. Your line was jews among muslims. Today, a room where that story was kept.

A shopping list. A child's alphabet practice, the letters wobbling across the page. A marriage contract. A merchant's letter complaining about a late ship. A page of poetry. A page of the Torah, worn soft. All of it in one dark room high in the wall of a synagogue in old Cairo, the Ben Ezra synagogue. Nobody meant it as an archive. People put papers there for one reason: they had God's name on them, or holy words, or Hebrew letters, and you don't throw that in the trash. So for centuries, the paper piled up.
screen: `A SHOPPING LIST, A CHILD'S ALPHABET.` → `A ROOM IN A CAIRO SYNAGOGUE.` → `YOU DON'T THROW IT IN THE TRASH.`

segments.voice: A geniza is a storeroom for worn-out holy writings. The idea is already in the Mishnah: in tractate Shabbat it says holy writings may be rescued from a fire, and that those which can't be read from are to be stored away. The Hebrew for that storing away is the same word, geniza. The custom grows from respect. A book with God's name in it is not just paper, so when a prayer book falls apart or a Torah scroll can no longer be read, it isn't thrown away. It's stored, and in time it may be buried, the way a person is. In Cairo, the pages stayed in the room, and the dry air seems to have kept them. Because people there seem to have put almost anything with Hebrew letters inside, the room ended up holding ordinary life: business letters, court records, recipes, prescriptions, love poems, and the handwriting of children learning to read. When scholars finally carried the papers out and began to read them, a world came back: merchants trading across seas, women in court over property, families writing to sons far away. That's the reason any of this survived: nothing holy thrown away. A habit of respect for words became, without anyone planning it, a memory for a whole community.
screen: `A STOREROOM FOR WORN HOLY WRITINGS.` · `THE MISHNAH: STORE THEM AWAY.` · `THE ROOM HELD ORDINARY LIFE.` · then, large: `NOTHING HOLY THROWN AWAY.`

916.title: The Karaites
916.hook: a movement that rejected the oral law and was argued with for centuries
916.howItsDone: Karaite communities still keep their own calendar, prayers and readings of the Torah, while Rabbanite Jews light Sabbath candles before sunset on Friday and let them burn into the evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cairo geniza, a room that kept a world because nothing holy was thrown away. Your line was nothing holy thrown away. Today, a disagreement you could find in those very papers.

Friday evening, just before the Sabbath. In one Jewish home, the candles are lit, and they'll burn through the evening, giving light to the meal. In another Jewish home, a Karaite home of an earlier age, the lamps go out before the Sabbath begins, and the family keeps the holy day in the dark. Both homes read the same verse of the Torah, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." Same verse. Both families Jewish. Two very different Friday nights, and the difference comes down to one question: is the written Torah enough on its own?
screen: `FRIDAY EVENING, TWO HOMES.` → `CANDLES BURNING, OR THE DARK.` → `IS THE WRITTEN TORAH ENOUGH?`

segments.voice: The Karaites are Jews who hold that the written Torah, the scripture itself, is the authority, and who do not accept the oral law of the Mishnah and Talmud as binding. Their name is usually explained from mikra, a Hebrew word for scripture, the text that is read. Tradition names Anan ben David as an early leader of the movement in Babylonia, and it grew in the lands we met this week. Back to the verse. The rabbinic tradition, the Rabbanites, reads it with the oral law: you may not kindle a fire on the Sabbath, but a light lit beforehand may keep burning. So, Sabbath candles. Karaite teachers, reading the verse on its own, took it to mean no fire may burn in the home on the Sabbath, even one lit before; Karaite practice today varies. Both sides were reading closely. They just started from different places. And they argued, for centuries. Saadia Gaon wrote against Karaite views, and Karaite scholars wrote back. The argument made both sides read harder: rely on scripture alone, and you need its Hebrew exactly; defend the oral law, and you have to show how it fits the written words. The book of Proverbs says, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "Iron sharpeneth iron," and the Talmud applies that verse to scholars who sharpen each other in study. Karaite communities still exist today, keeping their own way.
screen: `SCRIPTURE ALONE.` · `KINDLE NO FIRE: TWO READINGS.` · `SAADIA WROTE; KARAITES WROTE BACK.` · then, large: `IRON SHARPENETH IRON.`

917.title: Italy and Byzantium
917.hook: Jews have lived in Rome since before the Temple fell
917.howItsDone: Roman Jews and Romaniote Jews keep their own synagogue customs and prayer traditions, distinct from both Ashkenazi and Sephardi rites, and some still gather in historic synagogues in Rome and in Greece.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Karaites and the rabbis who argued back. Your line was argument sharpens. Today we head west, to a very old address.

In the Roman Forum stands a stone arch built for a general named Titus. Look up at the inside wall: carved soldiers carry a great lampstand on poles, the Temple menorah, out of a city they have just burned. A victory picture, made by the winners. Some Roman Jews keep a custom of never walking under that arch. And here's the strange part. Their community was in Rome before the arch went up, and it is still there now that the empire that built it is gone. Today, the old Jewish communities of Italy and Byzantium: people who stayed, generation after generation, in the same streets.
screen: `AN ARCH FOR TITUS.` → `A MENORAH CARRIED AWAY.` → `THE COMMUNITY THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: Start with the oldest written traces. The first book of Maccabees tells how Judah Maccabee sent envoys to Rome to make a treaty of friendship, before the Temple fell, and tradition in Rome's Jewish community points back to ties like it. Then the New Testament gives two snapshots. The book of Acts mentions a couple who had to leave the city, in the King James words, "because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome." And when Paul reaches Rome, Acts says he "called the chief of the Jews together." Even in stories about someone else, a Jewish community is already living there. Now turn east. When the Roman Empire split, its eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, is what historians call Byzantium. Greek-speaking Jews lived across its towns, in Greece, in the islands, and in southern Italy, which Byzantium ruled for a long stretch. Their descendants are sometimes called Romaniote Jews, and they kept their own prayer customs and poems. From southern Italy comes a Hebrew family chronicle, the Scroll of Ahimaaz: a writer traces his ancestors through generations of teachers, poets and community leaders, with miracle stories woven in. Life under Byzantine rule was not easy; the same scroll remembers an emperor who pressed Jews to convert, and times of hardship. But the communities held. And here's the thread for tomorrow: teachers and families from Italy carried learning north, over the Alps. An old community is a place that keeps handing things on.
screen: `ENVOYS TO ROME.` · then, large: `CALLED THE CHIEF OF THE JEWS TOGETHER.` · `GREEK-SPEAKING JEWS IN BYZANTIUM.` · `A FAMILY SCROLL THAT HANDS THINGS ON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the oldest community near you: a synagogue, a church, a mosque, a temple, a neighborhood that has kept its name. Who first gathered there, and what did they carry with them, a language, a recipe, a song? If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people who stayed.
